newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela boosts hydro-electric power with new dam.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela boosts hydro-electric power with new dam.

text.p: Energy-rich Venezuela, keen to be less dependent on abundant oil, expands its ambitious hydro-electric development along the Caroni river with the inauguration Thursday of the Macagua II power station.
The $2-billion project will bring 2,548 megawatts (MW) on line when all 14 turbines roar into operation before year-end.

Built and run by state-owned Electrificacion del Caroni CA (Edelca), Macagua II lies in eastern Guayana region near the Caroni's confluence with the Orinoco and 50 miles (80 km) downstream from Edelca's jewel, the massive Guri Dam.
Completed in 1986 with 20 turbines and capacity of 10,000 MW, Guri is the second largest hydro-electric generator in the world after the Itaipu dam in Brazil.

"Macagua II is a baby Guri, but quite a healthy one," an Edelca engineer said of the state-of-the art project which took nine years to build and is to be inaugurated by President Rafael Caldera, in presence of up to 2,000 special guests.
Edelca President Efrain Carrera told Reuters it was "part of long-term plans" to develop "the huge hydro-electric potential on the Caroni," an idea that was first conceived in 1953.
It will also allow Venezuela to extend a link across the border with Brazil and its potentially vast market.

Edelca has proposed a 455-mile (730-km) transmission line to the city of Boa Vista, capital of Roraima state, at an estimated cost of $110 million. An extension further south to Manaus is being contemplated.
"The idea is to meet energy demand in Roraima, of up to 200 MW per year ... We can provide them with energy at a convenient price," Carrera said, adding the link should be completed by December 1998.
Other projects along the Caroni include the Caruachi and Tocoma dams, to be completed in 2003 and 2007, with projected installed capacities of 2,160 MW each.
Edelca generates 73 percent of Venezuela's power, Carrera said, and enjoys access to relatively cheap power.
Venezuela's demand is currently 10,500 MW while Edelca installed capacity is 12,508 MW and long-term planned generating capacity from the Caroni will total nearly 26,000 MW.

"The cost per installed kilowatt is about $700 at Macagua, it was $460 at Guri," Works Manager Cesar Cardoso said during a tour of the plant. The figures compared favorably with an average $1,500 to $2,000 anywhere else in the world, he said.

These low costs were achieved thanks to a high flow along the Caroni, with an average 1.3 meter drop per kilometer, and a rocky river bed - mainly granite - that provided construction material on the site.

Macagua II will save Venezuela the equivalent of 76,000 barrels of oil per day, or $420 million a year at an average $15 per barrel, and earn the country up to $100 million per year, 20 percent of Edelca's total revenue.
